## Article

Ten patients from the TCGA liver hepatocellular carcinoma cohort, each contributing a tumour
sample and an adjacent normal one. Twenty libraries, ~60,000 genes measured by RNA
sequencing, and one question: which genes change between the two tissues.

The naive answer is thousands of them. The interesting part is what that answer leaves out.

## The confound

Before any testing, the counts get a variance-stabilising transform and a PCA. The first two
components should separate the conditions if the design is sound, and they do — normal
samples tight on one side at 18% of variance, tumours spread across the other.

That spread is the problem. Two of the ten patients are female, and the vertical structure in
the tumour cluster is partly gender. A model of condition alone is then not testing
condition; it is testing condition plus whatever gender happens to correlate with.

Refitting with `~ gender + condition` costs 107 genes: 5,778 significant before, 5,671 after
at a 5% false discovery rate. The estimate is that it matters less than the shape of the PCA
suggests, which is itself a result — a confound that is present but not dominant is different
from one that isn't there.

## The pathways that come back

The 5,671 genes get ranked by their test statistic and pushed through preranked GSEA against
the MSigDB biological-process collection, 15 to 500 genes per set. 865 gene sets come back
significant.

They are overwhelmingly cell cycle: chromosome segregation, nuclear chromosome segregation,
mitotic nuclear division, sister chromatid segregation, DNA replication, with normalised
enrichment scores around 2.3 to 2.85 and adjusted p-values below 10⁻³⁴. The direction is what
liver cancer biology predicts — a tumour that has lost differentiation and re-entered the
cell cycle.

Against that, the top negative enrichment scores are metabolic: organic acid catabolism,
small-molecule catabolism, fatty acid metabolism, at −2.6 to −3.0. Those are the processes
the normal liver does and the tumour stops doing.

Two coherent stories, pointing opposite ways, from one ranked list. A leading-edge gene from
the top set is NUF2, part of the NDC80 kinetochore complex that attaches chromosomes to
spindle microtubules; UBE2C and NEK2 are in the same short list, both mitotic.

## What it misses

DESeq2 tests genes. A gene can be equally abundant in both tissues and still be doing
something different — making a different isoform of the same transcript. That is differential
transcript usage, and it is invisible to a gene-level test by construction.

DEXSeq asks the other question. Counts per isoform, a generalised linear model with a
per-sample baseline and a per-isoform baseline, then a likelihood-ratio test of whether the
condition interacts with isoform identity:

```r
{{< include systems/chunks/06_dexseq_model.R >}}
```

Over 519 genes, 880 isoforms show significant usage shifts. The top five by adjusted
p-value are KHK, UGP2, CLEC1B, FN1 and GSTZ1 — fructose metabolism, glycogen precursor
synthesis, a platelet receptor, an extracellular matrix protein, and an oxidative-stress
enzyme. Liver-specific metabolism, immune recognition and tissue architecture, which is the
same story as the gene-level analysis told from a different angle.

## Where the two disagree

Collapsing isoform results to one row per gene, then re-adjusting the false discovery rate
across that new family, gives 15,312 genes tested by both methods. 1,947 are significant for
isoform usage, 4,594 for overall expression, and **843 in both**.

Fisher's exact test on the 2×2 table gives an odds ratio of about 2 and p = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴⁰.
Genes with differential usage are twice as likely as chance to also be differentially
expressed — a real association, and nowhere near a complete one. Each method finds signals
the other does not.

That gap is the point. Running the same GSEA on both gene rankings and plotting the normalised
enrichment scores against each other shows the answer at pathway level:

| | |
|---|---|
| Spearman correlation of NES | −0.082 |
| significant in both | a minority |
| pathways significant only in one | the majority |

A negative correlation between the two rankings means that for a great many pathways, the
gene-level analysis and the isoform-level analysis do not merely disagree on magnitude — they
disagree on direction. Not on the same pathways, but not in the same direction.

The conservative reading is that isoform-level testing is noisier and this is what noise looks
like. The reading I would defend is narrower: at the gene level, 5,671 genes separate tumour
from normal, and that number is an upper bound on how much of the biology the analysis
captured. The rest is in how the transcripts are put together.
